common_name: Dabney Pear (University of Tennessee Fire-Blight-Resistant Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; plant with a second pear cultivar for cross-pollination. Dabney was released from the University of Tennessee's fire-blight-resistant pear breeding program, the same program that produced Carrick and Morgan.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Dabney is a University of Tennessee fire-blight-resistant pear release combining moderate blight resistance with better-than-average dessert quality for a Southern-bred pear. The tree is small and spreading, becoming drooping under heavy crops, and bears early and heavily once established. Fruit is medium-sized, greenish with prominent russet dots, and the yellowish-white flesh is melting, tender, and juicy with a sweet-subacid flavor best suited to fresh eating rather than canning. Bloom comes in mid-to-late spring and fruit typically ripens in midsummer; harvest when fruit begins to soften at the blossom end, then ripen at room temperature.
sources: University of Tennessee historic pear breeding bulletins

common_name: Tenn Pear (Tennessee Pear, Fire-Blight-Resistant Low-Chill Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; plant with a second pear cultivar for cross-pollination, as Tenn is only partially self-fertile. Released from the same University of Tennessee fire-blight-resistant pear breeding program that produced Carrick, Morgan, Orient, and Ayers.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Tenn is one of the fire-blight-resistant pear releases from the University of Tennessee's historic breeding program, reported resistant to fire blight with moderate resistance to leaf spot and good heat tolerance once established. Its low-to-moderate chill requirement makes it workable in north and central Gulf Coast zone 8b-9a locations where many standard European pears fail to set fruit reliably. Trees bloom in early spring with fragrant white flowers and bear small, sweet, greenish-yellow pears with a red blush, best eaten fresh, ripening in early fall. Harvest when fruit begins to soften at the blossom end, then ripen at room temperature for best flavor.
sources: University of Tennessee historic pear breeding bulletins
